nodes.title: Amazon S3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: S3 is AWS's object store — flat namespace of buckets containing objects, accessed via HTTP. It backs almost every AWS architecture: data lakes, static sites, backups, lambda triggers, CloudFront origins. The exam tests storage classes, encryption, access control, and event notifications.

flashcards.front: S3 storage classes — pick one for backups, one for hot data, one for archive.
flashcards.back: Hot: S3 Standard (high cost, instant access). Backups / infrequent: S3 Standard-IA (cheaper storage, retrieval fee). Archive: Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest storage, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle policies move objects between classes automatically based on age.

flashcards.front: S3 bucket policy vs IAM policy vs ACL — which to use?
flashcards.back: IAM policy: 'this user/role can read bucket X'. Bucket policy: 'these principals can access this bucket' — required for cross-account and public access. ACL (legacy): per-object permissions, mostly avoided today. Use bucket policies for most cross-account, IAM for in-account.

flashcards.front: How do you make an S3 website (static-site hosting)?
flashcards.back: Enable static-website hosting on the bucket, upload index.html, set a bucket policy allowing public-read on objects, point a CloudFront distribution at it for HTTPS + edge caching. Don't expose the bucket directly — CloudFront with an OAC (Origin Access Control) is the canonical pattern.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between server-side and client-side encryption?
flashcards.back: SSE: data encrypted by S3 after upload. Variants: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed key, easiest), SSE-KMS (your KMS key, audit trail), SSE-C (you supply the key on each request). Client-side: you encrypt before upload — S3 only sees ciphertext. Pick SSE-KMS for compliance, SSE-S3 for default-on.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.
